children: By Sarah Spellings

Lily Balaisis started her business, Pink Palm Puff, with a hoodie in 2023. Known for sweatsuits featuring seashells, palm trees and embroidered phrases like "everything comes in waves," Pink Palm Puff, thanks to its teenage fans, has since become representative of another P-word: preppy.

To those who associate the term with navy blazers and chinos, that may come as a surprise. But ask teens what clothes constitute "preppiness" today, and Pink Palm Puff might come in the same breath as Ralph Lauren, Lilly Pulitzer and other labels that have long defined the look.

What started as a uniform of students on the campuses of elite schools has grown into a colorful, ever-expanding American style-one that over decades has been remixed in cities and beach towns, on runways and online.

Preppy style has also become hot again. Ralph Lauren sales have climbed-especially in Asia-outperforming some European luxury giants. Tommy Hilfiger's year-over-year revenue rose in the first quarter of 2026, and L.L. Bean is undergoing a significant U.S. retail expansion, adding seven locations last year and five so far in 2026. Three more are planned before the year's end.
Even as the preppy look has evolved, its underlying meaning hasn't changed, said Lisa Birnbach, editor of "The Official Preppy Handbook" published in 1980.

The satirical book, with lines like "it is the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child to wear khaki," is still a bible for preppy style. Birnbach's 2010 sequel, "True Prep," co-written with Chip Kidd, marveled at prep's journey to mass.

"The whole point about preppy is to feel at ease," Birnbach, 68, said in an interview. When her handbook was released, that was achieved by wearing worn-in Oxford shirts, corduroy pants and Sperry Top-Siders.
Now, it might mean wearing an Alo sweatsuit, printed pajamas and one of eight different versions of Miu Miu boat shoes.

"The different generations understand it differently," Birnbach said of preppy style. "What you're seeing with Generation Alpha," she added, "it's not really preppy in the way that I have defined it in the past, but it's not entirely not preppy, either."
Ivy Heritage: Worn-in, Buttoned-up and Classic
Before preppy became a term encompassing a broad sartorial universe, it started out as a word describing the wardrobes of students at college preparatory schools and Ivy League universities.

The release of "Love Story," the 1970 movie set at Harvard, pushed prep fully into popular culture. Ali MacGraw, who plays a working-class student, derisively uses "preppy" to describe her wealthy love interest played by Ryan O'Neal, who dresses in sport coats and thick cable-knit sweaters.
Birnbach's "The Official Preppy Handbook" further codified the style-its 10 fashion commandments promote values including conservatism, neatness, bright colors, sportiness and practicality.

Her handbook also democratized the style. "Looking, acting, and ultimately being prep is not restricted to an elite minority lucky enough to attend prestigious private schools," reads a line in its prologue.

Jason Jules, the author of the 2021 book "Black Ivy: A Revolt in Style," said that Black prep has existed almost as long as any other kind, citing Miles Davis and W.E.B Du Bois as examples of the style.
"There's this idea that Black people kind of flicked through GQ magazine or something and discovered this look," Jules, 62, said. "It's always been part and parcel of the African-American world."
Off-Campus Casual: Sporty, Coastal and Bright Colors

As a teen growing up in Chicago in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Reginald Jolley embraced a preppy style inspired by Ralph Lauren. He later co-founded Dem Dare, a group of party promoters who adopted a preppy-sporty aesthetic.
Many of its members, known as "Darians," blended labels like Polo Ralph Lauren, Lacoste, New Balance, United Colors of Benetton and Fila, said Jolley, an artist in his 50s who goes by Reggieknow.

"It has an aspirational thing to it," he said of the aesthetic favored by Darians. "That is like, opposite of the environment that I'm in, being on the West side of Chicago. The environment wasn't a preppy thing."

The early 2000s style of Kanye West, the artist who now goes by Ye, reflected the Darian style. When Ye, who also grew up in Chicago, released his album "The College Dropout" in 2004, he was known for wearing bright sweaters and vibrant polo shirts with popped collars.

As Birnbach pointed out, preppies have always loved color-often trading their navies and neutrals for cheerier shades when they decamped to vacation destinations like Georgia's Sea Island and Massachusetts's Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.
All are mentioned in "The Official Preppy Handbook," which has a chapter titled "Summer is a verb."

Another destination in Birnbach's handbook, Palm Beach, Fla., was where Lilly Pulitzer, a grand dame of preppy style, started her namesake line of brightly printed dresses in 1959. She is said to have conceived of them while working at a juice stand, with the aim of creating clothes that would disguise stains.
New Ivy: A Street, Runway, Luxury and Vintage Mashup
Starting in the mid 2010s, ascendant streetwear labels like Supreme and Vetements stole the spotlight-and market share-from those peddling prep.
Rugby Ralph Lauren, a diffusion line introduced in 2004, shuttered in 2013. York Street, a J. Press diffusion line, had an even shorter lifespan: It was in operation from 2012 to 2015.

Jack Carlson, 39, J.Press's president and creative director, came to the heritage brand after starting Rowing Blazers in 2017. It, along with brands like Noah and Aimé Leon Dore, turned preppy clothes into looser streetwear-giving preppiness new energy after it had fallen out of fashion.

Luxury European labels have furthered that momentum. They include Celine, whose creative director Michael Rider, a Ralph Lauren alum, has designed rugby sweaters, peacoats and his own take on boat shoes.

Peter Kuo, a 51-year-old New Yorker known as Preppy Pete to his over 26,000 followers on Instagram, has become a face of the new-school ivy look with outfits like blazers worn with loafers and Muay Thai shorts. Recently, Kuo was featured in an issue of the indie magazine Dozer, which aspired to make an updated version of "The Official Preppy Handbook."
Justinian Mason, the 29-year-old founder of Dozer, said the intention behind that issue of his magazine was to show "that prep is more accessible today."
Off-Campus Online: Preppy Turned Peppy

From around 2021 to 2024, prep became a TikTok trend, resulting in many of its modern affiliations-Pink Palm Puff hoodies, Golden Goose sneakers, Stoney Clover makeup bags with varsity-style patches and Roller Rabbit's monkey-printed pajamas.
One of the more inexplicable items associated with preppy style on TikTok was a pink Nirvana sweatshirt with the band's smiley face logo sold at Urban Outfitters.

All of the stuff was preppy because it was colorful and upbeat, said Anna Faye Rubenstein, an 18-year-old content creator and student in Washington, D.C., who started posting videos about the TikTok permutation of prep in 2023. "Some people say that this new preppy was meant to be peppy, but someone spelled it wrong," Rubenstein said.

Addison Willis, a 19-year-old student at Dartmouth, became smitten with the preppy style she started seeing on TikTok as a high-schooler outside of Dallas. When she moved to New Hampshire for college, she saw the traditional side of prep, marked by neutral tones and cable knits.
Willis still loves her Roller Rabbit pajamas, but is now incorporating more of the "New England chic girl" aesthetic into her wardrobe.
Pink Palm Puff has also embraced more muted tones-a recent collection included sweatshirts and shorts in navy and gray.

Rubenstein's TikTok videos include clips where she talks about the evolution of prep, playing characters from the '80s, '90s and 2000s. Immersing herself in preppy history has taught her that it "isn't a set style," she said. "It seems that it's a constantly evolving style that kind of just has been keeping the same name."
